source.title_on_document: Generative AI-Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self-Efficacy, and Flow State

supplement.holds: No separate supplementary material, online appendix, or supporting information is referenced in the complete 13-page document. The 'supplementary' student-AI interaction analysis is in the main text (Sections 3.4 and 4.4, Table 4; pp. 6-8). Group statistics are in Tables 1-3 (pp. 7-8); this PDF gives no standard errors or numerical pairwise post hoc statistics. Data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (p. 11, Data Availability Statement).

paper_design_summary: Seventy-eight fifth-grade students from three classes at one primary school in eastern China were randomly assigned to write 'Design Future Cars', an essay of about 300 words in 25 minutes, with Deepseek (20 students), with a peer (38 students in 19 pairs), or individually (20 students); all 78 were analyzed (p. 4, Section 3.1; pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2-3.3; p. 7, Table 1). Students handed in handwritten essays and immediately completed self-report flow and writing self-efficacy scales; three researchers later scored the essays on a 100-point rubric of originality (40 points), flexibility (30), and elaboration (30) (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2-3.4). An unaided baseline essay written one week earlier showed no statistically significant group difference (F = 2.56, p > 0.05; p. 4, Section 3.1).

studies.label: Classroom experiment: GenAI-supported vs peer-collaborative vs individual creative writing (fifth graders, China)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing condition for the week-2 creative writing task: GenAI-supported writing (Deepseek), peer-collaborative writing in pairs, or individual writing.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1 Participants; p. 1, Abstract (Methods); p. 5, Figure 1

arms.name: GenAI-supported writing group
arms.description: Each student used Deepseek on a computer during the 25-minute week-2 writing task, after an extra tutorial. The task sheet told students to use the AI as a thinking partner, evaluate its suggestions critically, and avoid verbatim copying. The final text was written by hand.

arms.name: Peer-collaborative writing group
arms.description: Students worked in pairs (19 pairs) to complete the writing task together by hand. The paper describes no AI use in this arm.

arms.name: Individual writing group
arms.description: Each student completed the writing task alone by hand. The paper describes no AI use in this arm.

participants.exclusions: None reported. No students or parents declined after the consent process (p. 4), and Table 1 reports N = 20, 38, and 20 (78 in all). The 38 peer-arm students wrote as 19 pairs, yet Tables 1 to 3 count 38; the paper does not say whether each pair produced one essay whose score was entered for both members.
participants.who: Fifth-grade primary school students aged 10-12 (M = 11, SD = 0.51), 42 boys (53.85 percent) and 36 girls (46.15 percent), from three classes of one school, all taught by the same teacher during the sessions. Recruited by convenience sampling; already highly familiar with GenAI tools from their regular learning.
participants.quote: A total of 78 students (aged 10–12 years; M = 11, SD = 0.51) from three classes were invited to participate in the study.

ai_tool.how_used: Short multi-turn chats with Deepseek on computers during the 25-minute task, as a 'thinking partner'. The logs hold 54 prompts; 4 off-task prompts were dropped, leaving 50 analyzed interaction episodes (2.50 prompts per student, range 1 to 8): idea generation 27 (54 percent), idea elaboration 10 (20 percent), writing support 10 (20 percent), other 3 (6 percent). Uptake: direct textual incorporation 8 (16 percent), adapted or selective 22 (44 percent), unclear 20 (40 percent). Final essays were handwritten (pp. 5-6, 8, Table 4).

task.description: Essay 'Design Future Cars' of around 300 words in week 2 (the scored outcome); a parallel essay, 'Design Future Shoes', written alone in week 1 served as the baseline. The task sheet gave no content guidance. The authors note that the task leaned toward expository and informational writing (p. 10).
task.duration: 25 minutes per essay; 8 minutes for the two questionnaires; 15-minute introductory course; the experiment lasted 2 weeks (p. 5, Figure 1).

outcomes.name: Creative writing performance (rubric total score, out of 100)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three researchers independently scored each handwritten week-2 essay on a rubric of Originality (40 points), Flexibility (30), and Elaboration (30), total 100; only the total is reported. Kendall's coefficient of concordance was 0.89 for week 2 and 0.57 for week 1. The paper's rule takes the three raters' average as the final score when reliability is high and resolves scores by discussion when it is low; the discussion-to-consensus meeting is described for the week-1 essays only (p. 6, Section 3.4). Rater blinding to condition is not stated. Analysis: one-way ANOVA (Levene 0.397 > 0.05) with LSD post hoc comparisons (p. 7). The paper reads GenAI-group scores as ratings of products of the student-AI process, not of unaided ability (p. 8).

outcomes.name: Writing self-efficacy (self-report, 6-point scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Writing Self-Efficacy Scale (Bruning et al. 2013): ideation (5 items), conventions (5), self-regulation (6), each rated 1 (not at all confident) to 6 (very confident); reliabilities 0.903, 0.847, 0.884. Answered right after the writing task. Welch's ANOVA (Levene 0.004 < 0.05) with LSD post hoc comparisons. A rating of the student's own confidence, not a score of the essay, so it does not meet criterion 3. AI availability during questionnaire completion is not reported (p. 5, Section 3.2 and Figure 1); the availability field is null because this self-report is not a scored creative output, and availability during its completion is unconfirmed.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: Section 3.1 explicitly states that participants were randomly assigned to GenAI-supported, peer-collaborative, or individual writing (p. 4); Deepseek was used during the assigned creative writing task (p. 5, Sections 3.2-3.3). The common unaided baseline precedes this between-person intervention. Criterion 2: 78 people were analyzed across the three arms: 20 GenAI, 38 peer-collaborative, and 20 individual (p. 7, Table 1; also Tables 2-3, pp. 7-8). The codebook applies the threshold across all study arms; the 38 peer-arm students count as people even though they worked in 19 pairs. Criterion 3: three researchers scored the handwritten essays on a 100-point creativity rubric, and Deepseek was available while the AI-arm essays were produced (pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2-3.4; p. 7, Table 1). The post-task self-report questionnaires do not qualify. Unreported randomization details, peer-score dependence, and rater blinding require clarification for appraisal or precision, but do not negate these reported eligibility facts.

one_line_finding: Fifth graders who wrote with Deepseek scored 88.850 (SD 1.420, n = 20) on a researcher-rated 100-point creative writing rubric, against 86.825 (SD 2.719, n = 38) for students writing in pairs and 85.133 (SD 2.120, n = 20) for students writing alone (one-way ANOVA F = 13.095, p = 0.000***; LSD a > b, a > c), p. 7, Table 1.
open_questions: Unit of randomization: the paper says participants were randomly assigned, but they came from three classes, and the arm sizes (20, 38, 20) are not explained. Were individuals randomized across classes, and how?

Peer arm: 19 pairs wrote, yet Tables 1 to 3 count N = 38. Did each pair produce one essay whose score was entered for both members? If so, the peer arm's 38 scores are not independent, which affects its SD, the omnibus F, and the LSD tests.
Raters were three of the researchers. The paper does not say whether they were blind to condition, although all final texts were handwritten.
Only the rubric total is reported; the originality, flexibility, and elaboration subscores are not.
Pairwise LSD comparisons are reported only as letter orderings (a > b, a > c, b > c), with no pairwise p-values, standard errors, or confidence intervals.
The week-1 (unaided) baseline scores by arm are not reported; only the omnibus test (F = 2.56, p > 0.05) is given (p. 4).
notes: Design coded field_rct because the sessions ran within regular classroom hours as standard pedagogical practice, in the computer laboratory where the classes held their regular computer lessons (pp. 4-5). Three researchers monitored the session, so lab_rct is a defensible alternative; both codes are core. S1-O2 (writing self-efficacy) and S1-O3 (flow state) are self-reports listed with question none; they do not bear on eligibility. Correlations: self-efficacy with creative writing performance r = 0.303, p = 0.007 (p. 7, Section 4.2); flow with performance r = −0.074, p = 0.521 (p. 8; the markdown misplaces the minus sign, the PDF prints it). Table 4 (p. 8) codes 50 student-AI interaction episodes descriptively and compares no arms. No outcome was measured after AI was removed, and no diversity outcome is reported. Table 1 prints p = 0.000***, while Section 4.1 reports p < 0.05. The paper cites the authors' related study (Yang, Liu, and Gao 2026, ETR&D) only for intervention length and states no shared participants. The PDF text layer omits the body text of Sections 4.1 to 4.3 on p. 7; those passages were checked on the page image. Final review: read the full markdown through the references (no appendices), checked source passages and all recorded numerical results in the PDF, and inspected Figure 1 plus the result passages missing from the PDF text layer. The two questionnaire-availability codes are null because availability at questionnaire completion is unreported and neither questionnaire is a scored creative output. The supplement status is not_stated because no separate supplement is referenced; this does not establish that none exists. The design summary now reflects questionnaire completion before later researcher scoring. All six existing open questions are classified in final.open_items; all reconciliation differences were already resolved. The reconciliation object is preserved as historical review.

open_items.item: Unit of randomization: the paper says participants were randomly assigned, but they came from three classes, and the arm sizes (20, 38, 20) are not explained. Were individuals randomized across classes, and how? Criterion 1 is met by the explicit participant-randomization statement (p. 4, Section 3.1). Author details on sequence generation, class handling, and allocation would settle implementation; this reporting gap does not make the stated random assignment unclear.

Peer arm: 19 pairs wrote, yet Tables 1 to 3 count N = 38. Did each pair produce one essay whose score was entered for both members? If so, the peer arm's 38 scores are not independent, which affects its SD, the omnibus F, and the LSD tests. Criterion 2 counts 78 analyzed people, including all 38 peer-arm students (p. 7, Table 1). Author clarification or participant-level data linking partners to essays and scores would settle dependence, which affects precision and the peer contrast rather than the people threshold.

Raters were three of the researchers. The paper does not say whether they were blind to condition, although all final texts were handwritten. Criterion 3 requires scoring of produced essays, which is explicitly reported (p. 6, Sections 3.3-3.4). The authors' rating protocol would settle blinding, a risk-of-bias question rather than an eligibility requirement.

Only the rubric total is reported; the originality, flexibility, and elaboration subscores are not. The reported rubric total already satisfies criterion 3 (p. 6, Section 3.4; p. 7, Table 1). Author-provided dimension-level summaries or scoring data would settle subscore extraction.

Pairwise LSD comparisons are reported only as letter orderings (a > b, a > c, b > c), with no pairwise p-values, standard errors, or confidence intervals. This concerns contrast precision rather than an eligibility criterion. Author-provided pairwise analysis output or data would supply the unreported statistics; the PDF provides letter orderings (pp. 7-8, Tables 1-3), and data are available on request (p. 11).

The week-1 (unaided) baseline scores by arm are not reported; only the omnibus test (F = 2.56, p > 0.05) is given (p. 4). This concerns baseline comparability rather than an eligibility criterion. Author-provided baseline summaries or data would settle the missing arm means and SDs; Section 3.1 (p. 4) reports only F = 2.56, p > 0.05. This pre-intervention task is not an after-AI outcome.
